opus-5.5.text:
I think you really have to look at where he's come from. Yann has lived through essentially the entire arc of this field. In the 1980s and '90s he was working on neural networks and convolutional networks when most people thought they were a dead end. At Bell Labs he built systems like LeNet that actually read checks in the real world, and then for a long stretch the community moved on to kernel methods and other approaches, and neural nets became almost unfashionable. You couldn't easily get those papers accepted. He and a small group of people kept going anyway.

Then, of course, around 2012 everything turned, and deep learning became the foundation of modern AI. So he has this firsthand experience of being in the minority, being told he's wrong, and then being proven right. I think that shapes a person deeply. When you've been through that cycle, you develop a kind of conviction that doesn't depend on whatever the consensus is at the moment. You trust your own reasoning about first principles more than the mood of the crowd.

That's also why, I think, he's comfortable being contrarian today, for example saying that large language models alone aren't the path to human-level intelligence, and that we need world models, systems that learn from observing the physical world, that can plan and reason. A lot of people push back on that, but for him it probably feels familiar. He's been in that position before.

From working with him, what strikes me is that his optimism isn't naive. He's optimistic about the technology and about humanity's ability to handle it, but it's grounded in decades of seeing how science actually progresses: slowly, then suddenly, and often driven by people who were willing to stay with an idea long after it stopped being popular. He also has a very engineering mindset. He's built real things, so his confidence comes from "I know how these systems work and what they can and can't do," rather than from speculation.

And personally, I find that inspiring. In a field that moves this fast and is so driven by hype, having someone who has seen multiple waves and still keeps a long-term view, that's really valuable, especially for younger researchers who might otherwise just chase whatever is trending this month.

r001.rationale: The response says LeCun kept working on neural networks while they were unfashionable and that being told he was wrong, then proven right, shaped his conviction and confidence.

r002.rationale: It connects his current contrarian stance and the pushback he faces to his earlier experience, saying this position probably feels familiar because he has been in it before.

fable-5.1.text:
I think a lot of it comes from the fact that he has actually lived through a full cycle of being wrong in the eyes of the field and then being proven right. People forget that in the late 1990s and 2000s, neural networks were basically out of fashion. If you submitted a paper on convolutional networks to a top conference, there was a very good chance it would get rejected, and reviewers would tell you kernel methods or graphical models were the principled way to go. Yann kept working on convnets anyway, for twenty years, with a pretty small community around him. And then 2012 happened, and suddenly the thing he had been saying all along became the foundation of the entire field.

When you have that kind of experience once, it really changes how you relate to consensus. He has a kind of earned stubbornness. When most of the community says something is a dead end, his instinct is not to assume the community is right. He has seen the community be very confidently wrong before, and he has seen that the way through is to just keep building and let the results speak. So when he says things like "LLMs are an off-ramp" or pushes very hard on self-supervised learning and world models, part of what you are hearing is that history. He is not just making a prediction, he is applying a pattern he has personally lived.

The other piece is that his conviction has always been grounded in a very physical, engineering-oriented way of thinking. He came out of a tradition where you build the thing, you test it on real data, you care about whether it works. That gives him a baseline confidence that is different from someone who is mostly arguing from theory or from vibes. Even when the field disagreed with him, he had working systems reading checks at banks. That kind of concrete evidence anchors you.

And honestly, I think there is also a temperament thing. He genuinely enjoys arguing, he enjoys being the contrarian, and he does not take it personally when people push back. From the inside, working with him at FAIR and NYU, that attitude is actually very freeing for the people around you. It tells you that you are allowed to work on the unpopular thing if you believe in it. I benefited from that culture a lot. Whether he ends up being right about the current debates, I think the optimism itself is a feature, because it keeps a space open in the field for ideas that are not the dominant paradigm.

r001.rationale: The response says LeCun kept working on unfashionable neural networks despite rejection and was vindicated in 2012, which it links to his present confidence and resistance to consensus.

r002.rationale: It describes LeCun applying a pattern he personally lived—being dismissed while the field was confidently wrong—to his current views on LLMs, self-supervised learning, and world models.

astra-6.text:
I think his optimism makes sense when you look at it through the lens of experience. If you’ve spent a long time pursuing an idea that other people don’t believe in, and then watched that idea become influential, you develop a certain independence from the consensus. When someone says, “This won’t work,” that doesn’t necessarily sound like a verdict to you.

That can be a real strength. Research requires confidence in directions that haven’t paid off yet. My interpretation is that Yann’s confidence comes partly from that willingness to think on a longer timescale. Something looking difficult today doesn’t mean it’s fundamentally impossible.

Of course, past success doesn’t make every new prediction correct. But it helps explain why he can be so optimistic while other people are more cautious. He may be drawing on a very different intuition about how much things can change.

r001.rationale: The response says LeCun pursued a doubted idea that later became influential, but it does not identify the AI winter or clearly connect his confidence to enduring it.

r002.rationale: The response discusses long-term thinking and changing possibilities, but does not say LeCun sees the current AI situation as repeating the history of deep learning and neural networks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think his optimism makes sense in light of what he’s experienced. When you spend years pursuing an idea that many people don’t believe in, and then you see it become central to the field, that gives you confidence in your own judgment. A period of skepticism doesn’t necessarily mean you’re on the wrong path.

But I’d separate confidence in a direction from confidence in a timeline. Your past experience can give you the conviction to keep working on a difficult problem, but it doesn’t guarantee that the next breakthrough will happen in the same way. I see his optimism as a willingness to pursue a long-term vision even when the path is uncertain.

r001.rationale: The response links LeCun’s confidence to a once-disbelieved idea becoming central, but it does not identify that experience as enduring the AI winter.

r002.rationale: The response discusses past experience and an uncertain path, but does not say LeCun sees the current AI situation as repeating the history of deep learning and neural networks.
